title: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is obvious that the incipient curvature of the arms, and consequently the form and direction of the spirals, will be influenced by the surrounding pressures, and these in turn by the general shape of the shell. We shall expect, accordingly, to find the long outwardly directed spirals associated with shells which are transversely elongated, as Spirifer is; while the more rounded Atrypas will tend to the opposite condition.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Spiral arms of Brachiopods”. Scope: spire-bearing brachiopods (Spiriferida, Atrypida, Athyridida and others)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The association is directly testable with fossil 3D morphology, including the named form classes. Demonstrating that pressure and available space cause the pattern is less discriminating than documenting the predicted correlation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct shell interior and brachidium geometry across spire-bearing brachiopods, quantify shell elongation and flattening, and test the predicted association with outward, inward or discoid spiral direction. Phylogenetically controlled models should compare spatial constraint with clade-specific development.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Internal brachidia are incompletely preserved.

Shell shape and arm direction are strongly confounded with phylogeny.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.6

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted association of spiral direction with shell shape is checkable from illustrated and scanned brachiopods, and those resources exist for the classical genera. They do not record the pressures inside the shell, so the causal clause is not directly measured. Phylogenetic conservatism can produce the same association, which limits how far a positive table would establish the mechanical explanation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Pair brachidial spiral direction and form with shell outline across spire-bearing brachiopods: outward spirals with transverse shells such as Spirifer, inward spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with flattened shells. The association is supported or refuted by that cross-tabulation; the pressure mechanism remains an interpretation of the association.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Spiral direction and shell shape can be conserved together by ancestry rather than by spatial constraint.

Many specimens preserve the shell outline without the brachidium, so the paired sample is smaller than shell collections.
